title: The revised cue sheet for The Winter Switch
public_context: A producer's marked script and control-room note describe the making of a fictional radio drama. The document follows the general work of shaping a story for listeners without a visible stage. It reads as a production record in a familiar broadcast setting, rather than a review of a finished program.
source_title: Director's control-room note on The Winter Switch
source_text:
The radio drama The Winter Switch was commissioned as a nineteen-minute play for the Bellwether service. I kept its rehearsal copy beside one gray cue sheet because the story moves between a present-day room and a winter remembered by its caretaker. In the first draft, a small brass bell sounded at the opening of the play and at every return to memory. There were four scenes, and the bell appeared at the opening of scenes two, three, and four. The copy gave no spoken date for those returns.

At open rehearsal, three script readers thought each bell introduced a new location rather than an earlier time. They could follow the plot, but one asked why the caretaker had traveled so quickly. The writer and I agreed not to add an explanatory narrator. Instead, we added a repeated version of the line “Leave the cup beside the blue tile” at the end of scene two. Her sister first spoke it in scene one; the caretaker repeats the same words at the end of scene two, so the remembered time has an audible echo without removing the sister's earlier line.

On recording day, the two actors completed all four scenes. The sister's line was recorded with the scene-one room tone, and the caretaker's repeated line was recorded for the end of scene two. We kept a short pause before the repeat so it would be heard as an echo of an earlier conversation, not as a reply from off-mic. The bell remained at the opening of scene one; it was removed from all later transitions. All voices sat in the center of the single-channel mix, and the bell was not moved between speakers.

The broadcast desk had asked for a single-channel master, so the control room did not use left-right placement to distinguish the two periods. No telephone feed was connected during the session; the sister's line was performed in the studio. After playback, the producer returned one timing note: keep the quiet after the repeated line, with no words or effects under it. The final reel ran nineteen minutes and twelve seconds and went to the service's scheduling desk with the revised cue sheet. No audience check followed this recording. I filed the marked script in the finished-plays drawer and put the old cue sheet in the recycling tray.
